\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The measurement}
A computational pipeline produces, for each integer input $x$, a scalar \emph{rate}. Two cheap arithmetic summaries of $x$ compete to predict it: the \emph{trailing-zero statistic} $T(x)=\nu_2(x)$, the largest $k$ with $2^k\mid x$; and the \emph{popcount baseline} $W(x)$, the number of one-bits of $x$. In the experiment under discussion, integers were drawn uniformly among those of exactly $48$ bits, i.e.\ uniformly on the dyadic window $[2^{47},2^{48})$, and the Spearman rank correlation between $T$ and the rate was recorded across three independent seeds:
\[
0.7291,\qquad 0.7286,\qquad 0.7087,
\]
all inside a pre-registered validation band $[0.55,0.85]$. The pooled advantage of $T$ over $W$ was $+0.134$ with confidence interval $[0.113,0.158]$. Across widening sampling regimes the dial declines roughly $0.78\to0.72\to0.65\to0.61$.

\subsection{The deflationary hypotheses}
Both statistics are heavily tied: $T$ takes the value $0$ on half of all integers, $1$ on a quarter, and so on, and ties cap rank correlation. Four deflationary hypotheses present themselves.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(H1)] \emph{Saturation.} The value $\approx0.73$ is simply the ceiling imposed by ties.
\item[(H2)] \emph{Quantisation drift.} The decline with bit-length is the ceiling moving.
\item[(H3)] \emph{Tie-geometric advantage.} $T$ beats $W$ because $T$ has more headroom.
\item[(H4)] \emph{Window effects.} The seed spread reflects where the sampling window sits.
\end{itemize}
Each is a statement about the \emph{tie profile} of the statistic, a purely arithmetic object. We compute those profiles exactly and settle all four.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item A closed-form tie ceiling $\tfrac67\bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{2^b(2^b+1)}\bigr)$ for the trailing-zero statistic, with the constant $6/7$ arising as a dyadic geometric series (Theorem~\ref{thm:dyadicceiling}).
\item The one-bit shift law: exact-bit-length conditioning shifts \emph{both} tie profiles down by exactly one bit, so all comparisons transport (Theorems~\ref{thm:shiftzero} and \ref{thm:shiftpop}).
\item Full translation invariance with no error term (Theorem~\ref{thm:translation}), specialising to the aligned case (Theorem~\ref{thm:aligned}).
\item The cube-sum reduction and the exact inversion threshold $b\ge3$, with sharpness at $b\in\{1,2\}$ (Theorems~\ref{thm:criterion}, \ref{thm:threshold}, \ref{thm:sharp}).
\item An odd-parity Franel estimate and its transfer to a ceiling bound (Theorems~\ref{thm:franelodd}, \ref{thm:transfer}).
\item Refutation of (H1)--(H4) for the recorded measurement (Section~\ref{sec:application}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Preliminaries: tie profiles and the Spearman ceiling}

\begin{definition}[Tie profile]
Let $f$ be a statistic on a finite sample $S$ with $|S|=n$. Its \emph{tie profile} is the multiset of fibre cardinalities $(m_1,\dots,m_r)$, $m_j=|f^{-1}(v_j)|$ over the distinct attained values. Its \emph{mass} is $n=\sum_j m_j$ and its \emph{cube sum} is $C=\sum_j m_j^3$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Ceiling functional]
For a profile $L=(m_1,\dots,m_r)$ of mass $n\ge2$,
\[
\Sp(L)\;=\;1-\frac{\sum_j m_j^3-n}{n^3-n}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Interpretation]
$\Sp(L)$ is the supremum, over all responses $Y$ on the sample, of the squared Spearman rank correlation of $f$ against $Y$; the supremum is attained by any $Y$ strictly monotone in $f$ up to arbitrary within-block ordering.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Sketch]
With mid-ranks inside each tied block, the rank vector of $f$ has variance $\tfrac{n^3-n}{12}-\tfrac{1}{12}\sum_j(m_j^3-m_j)$ instead of the untied $\tfrac{n^3-n}{12}$. Cauchy--Schwarz against the response's rank vector, of variance at most $\tfrac{n^3-n}{12}$, gives $\rho^2\le\Sp(L)$, with equality for an untied order-compatible response.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cube-sum reduction]\label{lem:cubereduce}
$\Sp(L)$ depends on $L$ only through its mass $n$ and cube sum $C$: $\Sp(L)=1-\frac{C-n}{n^3-n}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Order reversal]\label{thm:reversal}
Let $L,M$ be profiles of equal mass $n\ge2$. Then
\[
\text{(i) } C(M)<C(L)\ \Longrightarrow\ \Sp(L)<\Sp(M);\qquad
\text{(ii) } C(L)=C(M)\ \Longrightarrow\ \Sp(L)=\Sp(M).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$n^3-n=n(n-1)(n+1)>0$ for $n\ge2$, and $\Sp$ is a strictly decreasing affine function of $C$ at fixed $n$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:reversal} is the methodological lesson: \emph{compare cube sums, not ceilings}. The map $C\mapsto\Sp$ is an order-reversing bijection at fixed mass, and all combinatorial estimates are cleaner upstream of it.

\begin{definition}[The two profiles]
The \emph{dyadic profile} is $D_b=(2^{b-1},2^{b-2},\dots,2,1,1)$ of length $b+1$: entry $k$ is $2^{b-1-k}$ for $0\le k<b$, and the final entry is $1$. The \emph{binomial profile} is $B_b=\bigl(\binom{b}{0},\dots,\binom{b}{b}\bigr)$. Both have mass $2^b$. The \emph{Franel number} is $\franel(b)=\sum_{j=0}^b\binom{b}{j}^3$, with values $1,2,10,56,346,2252,15184,\dots$
\end{definition}

\section{The dyadic profile and its closed-form ceiling}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:blocks}
For $k<b$, the set $A_{b,k}=\{x<2^b:\ 2^k\mid x,\ 2^{k+1}\nmid x\}$ has cardinality $2^{b-1-k}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Its elements are exactly $2^k(2t+1)<2^b$, i.e.\ $t<2^{b-1-k}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:dyadicprofile}
The tie profile of $\nu_2$ on $[0,2^b)$ is $D_b$ (the remaining point being $x=0$), of mass $2^b$ and cube sum
\[
C(D_b)=\sum_{k=0}^{b-1}8^{\,b-1-k}+1=\frac{8^b-1}{7}+1 .
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Dyadic ceiling]\label{thm:dyadicceiling}
For $b\ge1$,
\[
\Sp(D_b)=\frac{6}{7}\left(1+\frac{1}{2^b(2^b+1)}\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $n=2^b$, so $C=\frac{n^3-1}{7}+1$ and $C-n=\frac{n^3-7n+6}{7}=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)(n+3)}{7}$, while $n^3-n=n(n-1)(n+1)$. Hence
\[
\Sp(D_b)=1-\frac{(n-2)(n+3)}{7n(n+1)}=\frac{7n(n+1)-(n^2+n-6)}{7n(n+1)}
=\frac{6(n^2+n+1)}{7n(n+1)}=\frac67\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{n(n+1)}\Bigr).\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Envelope]\label{cor:envelope}
For $b\ge1$: $\tfrac67<\Sp(D_b)\le\tfrac67+2^{-b}$ and $\Sp(D_b)-\tfrac67<4^{-b}$; moreover $b\mapsto\Sp(D_b)$ is strictly decreasing.
\end{corollary}

Thus $\rho_{\max}=\sqrt{\Sp(D_b)}\to\sqrt{6/7}=0.925820\ldots$ extremely fast: at $b=47$ the correction is below $10^{-28}$.

\section{Exact-bit-length conditioning: the one-bit shift law}

Uniform sampling at exact bit-length $b+1$ means uniform sampling on $\mathcal W_b=[2^b,2^{b+1})$, a strictly different measure from uniform on $[0,2^{b+1})$.

\begin{theorem}[One-bit shift, trailing zeros]\label{thm:shiftzero}
For $k<b$, exactly $2^{b-1-k}$ elements of $\mathcal W_b$ satisfy $\nu_2=k$, and exactly one, namely $2^b$, satisfies $\nu_2=b$. Hence the tie profile of $\nu_2$ on uniform draws of exact bit-length $b+1$ is exactly $D_b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The $k$-th block of $\mathcal W_b$ is $A_{b+1,k}\setminus A_{b,k}$, of size $2^{b-k}-2^{b-1-k}=2^{b-1-k}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:blocks}. An element of $\mathcal W_b$ divisible by $2^b$ is $2^bu$ with $2^b\le 2^bu<2^{b+1}$, forcing $u=1$. Assembling gives $(2^{b-1},\dots,2,1,1)=D_b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One-bit shift, popcount]\label{thm:shiftpop}
The number of integers of exact bit-length $b+1$ with popcount $j+1$ is $\binom{b}{j}$. Hence the popcount tie profile on exact bit-length $b+1$ is exactly $B_b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Identify such integers with subsets $S\subseteq\{0,\dots,b\}$ containing $b$. Then $S\mapsto S\setminus\{b\}$ is a bijection onto the $j$-subsets of $\{0,\dots,b-1\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Comparisons transport]
Conditioning on exact bit-length $b+1$ replaces both tie profiles by their full-range bit-length-$b$ counterparts; every ceiling comparison at bit-length $b$ holds verbatim at exact bit-length $b+1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}
For $b\ge1$, $\Sp(D_{b+1})<\Sp(D_b)$ and $\Sp(D_b)-\Sp(D_{b+1})<4^{-b}$: exact-bit-length conditioning strictly raises the trailing-zero ceiling, by an amount undetectable at any realistic sample size.
\end{corollary}

\section{Invariance: the profile does not see the window}

\subsection{Aligned windows}

\begin{lemma}[Translation of low valuations]\label{lem:translate}
Let $\mathcal A_{c,s}=[c2^s,(c+1)2^s)$. For $k<s$, the map $x\mapsto x+c2^s$ is a bijection from the $k$-th block of $[0,2^s)$ onto the $k$-th block of $\mathcal A_{c,s}$; consequently that block has $2^{s-1-k}$ elements. The set of multiples of $2^s$ in $\mathcal A_{c,s}$ is the singleton $\{c2^s\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $k<s$ both $2^k$ and $2^{k+1}$ divide $2^s$, so adding $c2^s$ preserves and reflects both divisibility conditions. If $2^su\in\mathcal A_{c,s}$ then $c\le u<c+1$, i.e.\ $u=c$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dyadic-scale invariance]\label{thm:aligned}
For all $c,s$ the trailing-zero tie profile of $\mathcal A_{c,s}$ is exactly $D_s$; hence all aligned windows of a common scale share the ceiling $\tfrac67\bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{2^s(2^s+1)}\bigr)$, independently of $c$.
\end{theorem}

The exact-bit-length window is $c=1$ and the full range is $c=0$, recovering Theorem~\ref{thm:shiftzero} and Proposition~\ref{prop:dyadicprofile}.

\subsection{Arbitrary windows}

\begin{lemma}[Valuation as a residue class]\label{lem:residue}
For all $k,x$: $\ x\equiv 2^k \pmod{2^{k+1}}$ if and only if $2^k\mid x$ and $2^{k+1}\nmid x$, i.e.\ $\nu_2(x)=k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $x=2^{k+1}q+2^k=2^k(2q+1)$ then $2^k\mid x$ and $2^{k+1}\nmid x$. Conversely if $x=2^ku$ with $u=2q+1$ odd, then $x=2^{k+1}q+2^k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Equidistribution in a run]\label{lem:equidist}
For all $A,M,v$ and $r\ge1$, $\bigl|\{x\in[A,A+Mr):x\equiv v \pmod r\}\bigr|=M$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The interval is a disjoint union of $M$ blocks of $r$ consecutive integers, each a complete residue system mod $r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Translation invariance]\label{thm:translation}
For every $A$ and $s$: for each $k<s$ exactly $2^{s-1-k}$ elements of $[A,A+2^s)$ satisfy $\nu_2=k$, and exactly one is divisible by $2^s$. Hence the trailing-zero tie profile of \emph{any} window of $2^s$ consecutive integers is exactly $D_s$, with ceiling $\tfrac67\bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{2^s(2^s+1)}\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $k<s$ and write $2^s=2^{s-1-k}\cdot 2^{k+1}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:residue} the $k$-th block is $\{x\in[A,A+2^{s-1-k}2^{k+1}) : x\equiv 2^k \pmod{2^{k+1}}\}$, of size $2^{s-1-k}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:equidist}. For the cap take $M=1$, $r=2^s$, $v=0$. Since $\sum_{k<s}2^{s-1-k}+1=2^s$, these blocks exhaust the window.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Complete invariance]
The trailing-zero tie ceiling is a function of the sample size $2^s$ alone: independent of the magnitude of the integers, of bit-length conditioning, of alignment to a dyadic grid, and of the placement of the window.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
The natural conjecture that non-aligned windows perturb the profile at order $\Theta(2^{-s})$ is false, and not merely to leading order: there is no error term at all. The aligned proof is structurally transparent but proves less than the shorter residue-counting proof --- proving the general statement removed the hypothesis that made the special case look delicate.
\end{remark}

\section{The inversion threshold}

Both $D_b$ and $B_b$ have mass $2^b$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:reversal} everything reduces to cube sums:
\[
C(D_b)=\frac{8^b-1}{7}+1,\qquad C(B_b)=\franel(b).
\]

\begin{theorem}[Arithmetic inversion criterion]\label{thm:criterion}
For $b\ge1$,
\[
\Sp(D_b)<\Sp(B_b)\iff C(B_b)<C(D_b)\iff 7\franel(b)<8^b+6 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Coarse Franel bound]\label{lem:coarse}
$\franel(b)\le\binom{b}{\lfloor b/2\rfloor}^2 2^b$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Odd middle binomial]\label{lem:oddmid}
$\binom{2m+1}{m}\le 2\binom{2m}{m}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Pascal gives $\binom{2m+1}{m}=\binom{2m}{m-1}+\binom{2m}{m}$, and both terms are at most the row maximum $\binom{2m}{m}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Odd Franel estimate]\label{thm:franelodd}
For all $m\ge0$, $\ \franel(2m+1)(3m+1)\le 8^{2m+1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemmas~\ref{lem:coarse} and \ref{lem:oddmid}, $\franel(2m+1)\le\bigl(2\binom{2m}{m}\bigr)^2 2^{2m+1}$. Multiplying by $3m+1$ and using $\binom{2m}{m}^2(3m+1)\le 16^m$,
\[
\franel(2m+1)(3m+1)\le 4\cdot16^m\cdot2^{2m+1}=2^{2}\cdot2^{4m}\cdot2^{2m+1}=2^{6m+3}=8^{2m+1}.\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Franel-to-ceiling transfer]\label{thm:transfer}
Let $b\ge1$ and $c>0$ with $\franel(b)\,c\le 8^b$. Then $\Sp(B_b)\ge 1-\frac2c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $n=2^b$ and $n^3=8^b$, Lemma~\ref{lem:cubereduce} gives $\Sp(B_b)=1-\frac{\franel(b)-n}{8^b-n}$. Since $\franel(b)\le 8^b/c$,
\[
\frac{\franel(b)-n}{8^b-n}\le\frac{8^b/c-n}{8^b-n}\le\frac2c,
\]
the last step because $c(8^b/c-n)\le 2(8^b-n)$ rearranges to $n(2-c)\le 8^b$, valid since $n(2-c)\le 2n=2^{b+1}\le 8^b$ for $b\ge1$.
\end{proof}

Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer} with $b=2m+1$, $c=3m+1$ gives $\Sp(B_{2m+1})\ge 1-\frac{2}{3m+1}$. Combined with $\Sp(D_b)\le\frac67+2^{-b}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:envelope}), for $m\ge5$,
\[
\Sp(D_{2m+1})\le\tfrac67+\tfrac{1}{1024}<\tfrac78\le\Sp(B_{2m+1}),
\]
the odd half of the inversion law; the even half follows from the corresponding even estimate by the same transfer. Together they cover all $b\ge10$.

The estimate is too lossy below $b=10$ (at $b=8$ it yields only $1-2/13=0.846<6/7$), but there the criterion is finite arithmetic:

\begin{theorem}[Inversion threshold]\label{thm:threshold}
For every $b\ge3$, $\ \Sp(D_b)<\Sp(B_b)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $3\le b\le 9$ the table verifies $7\franel(b)<8^b+6$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:criterion} applies. For $b\ge10$ split by parity and apply the odd estimate (Theorem~\ref{thm:franelodd} with $m\ge5$) or its even counterpart.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]\label{thm:sharp}
$\Sp(D_1)=\Sp(B_1)$ and $\Sp(D_2)=\Sp(B_2)$; hence for $b\ge1$, $\ \Sp(D_b)<\Sp(B_b)\iff b\ge3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$D_1=(1,1)=B_1$, and $D_2=(2,1,1)$, $B_2=(1,2,1)$ are permutations of one another, so they have equal mass and cube sum; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:reversal}(ii). Equivalently $7\franel(1)=14=8+6$ and $7\franel(2)=70=64+6$. Combine with Theorem~\ref{thm:threshold}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:inv48}
For $b\ge3$, on uniform draws of exact bit-length $b+1$ the popcount baseline has strictly greater tie headroom than the trailing-zero statistic. In particular this holds at exact bit-length $48$, where both profiles are the bit-length-$47$ ones.
\end{corollary}

Bit-lengths $1$ and $2$ are thus the only regimes where the two statistics are tie-equivalent; above them the geometry always favours the popcount baseline, uniformly and without asymptotics.

\section{Application: the recorded measurement}\label{sec:application}

Write $\rho_{10}=0.7291$, $\rho_{11}=0.7286$, $\rho_{12}=0.7087$, pooled $\bar\rho=0.72213\overline3$, advantage $\Delta=0.134$ with CI $[0.113,0.158]$, and implied pooled baseline $\bar\rho-\Delta=0.58813\overline3$.

\begin{proposition}[Band]
All three seeds satisfy $0.55<\rho_i<0.85$, as does the implied baseline; the seed spread is $\rho_{10}-\rho_{12}=0.0204<0.021$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[No saturation --- refutes (H1)]
At exact bit-length $48$ the ceiling is $\Sp(D_{47})=\tfrac67\bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{2^{47}(2^{47}+1)}\bigr)>\tfrac67$, i.e.\ $\rho_{\max}=0.92582\ldots$, whereas $\rho_i^2\le 0.7291^2=0.5316<\tfrac67$ for every seed.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[No quantisation drift --- refutes (H2)]
$\Sp(D_{47})-\Sp(D_{64})<4^{-47}<10^{-28}$, while the recorded dial moves by more than $0.07$ over the same change of regime.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:envelope} bounds $\Sp(D_{47})-\tfrac67<4^{-47}$, and $\Sp(D_{64})>\tfrac67$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Advantage is signal --- refutes (H3)]
At exact bit-length $48$ the popcount baseline has the strictly larger ceiling (Corollary~\ref{cor:inv48}), yet the measurement places the trailing-zero statistic $+0.134$ above it: the measured ordering reverses the tie-headroom ordering.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Window placement is inert --- refutes (H4)]
Every window of $2^{47}$ consecutive integers --- the exact-bit-length-$48$ window, any aligned window, any unaligned window, and the full range $[0,2^{47})$ --- has the identical ceiling $\tfrac67\bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{2^{47}(2^{47}+1)}\bigr)$ by Theorems~\ref{thm:aligned} and \ref{thm:translation}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{corollary}[Factorisation]
Writing $\rho=\rho_{\mathrm{ceiling}}\cdot\rho_{\mathrm{response}}$, the first factor is pinned exactly and flat to $O(4^{-s})$ across all windows, scales, placements and bit-length conditionings. All observed variation --- the decline $0.78\to0.72\to0.65\to0.61$, the seed spread, and the $+0.134$ advantage --- lives in $\rho_{\mathrm{response}}$; any explanatory model must be response-side.
\end{corollary}

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{A. Profile of an arbitrary window.} Given $A$ and $s$, the trailing-zero tie profile of $[A,A+2^s)$ is computed without enumeration in $O(s)$ arithmetic operations: block $k<s$ has size $2^{s-1-k}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:equidist} and the cap has size $1$. Naive enumeration costs $\Theta(2^s)$.

\paragraph{B. Ceiling from a profile.} Given a profile of mass $n$, evaluate $\Sp=1-\frac{C-n}{n^3-n}$ in exact rational arithmetic in $O(r)$ operations; for $D_s$ the closed form of Theorem~\ref{thm:dyadicceiling} avoids the sum entirely.

\paragraph{C. Inversion decision.} Evaluate $7\franel(b)<8^b+6$. Computing $\franel(b)$ costs $O(b)$ big-integer multiplications on $O(b)$-bit numbers, i.e.\ $\tilde O(b^2)$ bit operations; asymptotically Theorem~\ref{thm:franelodd} decides the question in $O(1)$.

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{What the invariance buys.} Four knobs are proved inert: integer magnitude, bit-length conditioning, window alignment, window placement. These are not small effects but exactly zero effects, up to the explicit $O(4^{-s})$ term coming from sample size alone --- unusual, because applied invariance statements normally carry an error term. Here the mechanism is exact residue equidistribution.

\paragraph{Work upstream of the ceiling map.} Every comparison in the inversion section became tractable only after being pushed into a statement about $\sum_j m_j^3$, where Franel numbers and geometric series live and the classical inequality toolkit applies. Direct ceiling bounds of the form $\Sp\ge1-2/c$ are provably insufficient in the small range: at $b=8$ the best such bound gives $0.846<6/7$ and cannot decide a comparison that is nonetheless true.

\paragraph{The constant $6/7$.} It arises because the dyadic profile halves geometrically. Any statistic whose tie blocks decay by a fixed ratio $q$ has an analogous limiting ceiling; the trailing-zero statistic is the case $q=1/2$. This suggests a family of geometric dials with tunable, prescribed headroom.

\paragraph{Limitations.} The ceiling is an upper bound over all responses: it certifies that $0.73$ is not forced, but cannot predict it. The analysis assumes exactly $2^s$ consecutive integers; for $N$ not a power of two the profile acquires computable boundary corrections (Lemma~\ref{lem:equidist} with $M=\lfloor N/2^{k+1}\rfloor$ plus a remainder). Sampling with replacement makes block sizes multinomial, so the ceiling becomes a random variable concentrated at the deterministic value.

\section{Future directions}

\paragraph{Response-side attenuation law.} The measured coefficient factorises as $\rho=\rho_{\mathrm{ceiling}}\cdot\rho_{\mathrm{response}}$ with the first factor now pinned exactly; the decline $0.78\to0.72\to0.65\to0.61$ must live entirely in the second. Identifying its functional form, and proving it forced by the response's own structure rather than by the sampler, is the outstanding problem.

\paragraph{Non-power-of-two windows.} Extend translation invariance to length $N$: block sizes become $\lfloor N/2^{k+1}\rfloor$ or one more according to phase, so the ceiling oscillates with $N\bmod 2^{k+1}$, presumably at order $1/N$.

\paragraph{Geometric dials with prescribed ceilings.} For blocks decaying with ratio $q=1/p$ (the $p$-adic valuation), compute the limiting ceiling and characterise attainable values; $p=2$ recovers $6/7$.

\paragraph{Sharper Franel comparisons.} The asymptotics $\franel(b)\sim c\,8^b/b$ suggest the criterion holds with multiplicative margin $\Theta(b)$, giving a quantitative rather than qualitative inversion.

\paragraph{Beyond two statistics.} Digit sums in other bases, run lengths and low-order residues can all be placed on a single totally ordered scale of headroom by computing their tie profiles and cube sums, telling an experimenter in advance which coarse statistic can in principle correlate best.

\section{Conclusion}

The tie geometry of the trailing-zero statistic is completely rigid. On any $2^s$ consecutive integers --- anywhere, at any magnitude, aligned or not, bit-length conditioned or not --- the tie profile is exactly $(2^{s-1},\dots,2,1,1)$ and the ceiling is exactly $\tfrac67\bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{2^s(2^s+1)}\bigr)$. Against the popcount baseline, whose ceiling is governed by Franel numbers, the trailing-zero statistic has strictly less headroom at every bit-length $b\ge3$ and exactly equal headroom at $b\in\{1,2\}$. Applied to the recorded measurement this closes four explanatory routes at once, leaving a well-posed question about the response, unclouded by the arithmetic of the sampler.

Tie geometry of the trailing-zero statistic: numerical demonstrations.

This self-contained script verifies, by direct computation, every quantitative
claim of the accompanying paper:

  1. The trailing-zero tie profile of a window of 2^s consecutive integers is
     exactly D_s = (2^(s-1), ..., 2, 1, 1), for ANY starting point.
  2. The closed-form ceiling  Sp(D_b) = (6/7) * (1 + 1/(2^b (2^b + 1))),
     and its convergence to 6/7 at rate O(4^-b).
  3. The one-bit shift law: uniform draws at exact bit-length b+1 have
     trailing-zero profile D_b and popcount profile B_b.
  4. The cube-sum reduction and the exact inversion threshold b >= 3, with
     equality of ceilings at b = 1, 2.
  5. The recorded measurement (seeds 0.7291 / 0.7286 / 0.7087, advantage
     +0.134) checked against the theory.
  6. A Monte-Carlo sanity check that the ceiling really is attained by an
     order-compatible response and never exceeded by an arbitrary one.

Only the standard library is used; all arithmetic on ceilings is exact
(fractions.Fraction).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from fractions import Fraction
from math import comb
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Basic statistics
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def trailing_zeros(x: int) -> int:
    """The 2-adic valuation nu_2(x): number of trailing binary zeros.

    By convention nu_2(0) is treated as 'maximal' by the caller; here we
    return the number of trailing zeros of the binary expansion, and 0 is
    handled explicitly by the profile routines.
    """
    if x == 0:
        raise ValueError("nu_2(0) is infinite; handle 0 separately")
    return (x & -x).bit_length() - 1


def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    """Number of one-bits in the binary expansion of x."""
    return bin(x).count("1")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Tie profiles and the Spearman ceiling
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def profile_of(values: Sequence[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Tie profile: the sorted list of fibre sizes of a statistic's values."""
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for v in values:
        counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1
    return [counts[k] for k in sorted(counts)]


def cube_sum(profile: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Sum of cubes of the block sizes."""
    return sum(m ** 3 for m in profile)


def spearman_ceiling(profile: Sequence[int]) -> Fraction:
    """Maximal attainable squared Spearman coefficient for this tie profile.

    Sp(L) = 1 - (sum_j m_j^3 - n) / (n^3 - n),  n = sum_j m_j >= 2.
    """
    n = sum(profile)
    if n < 2:
        raise ValueError("profile mass must be at least 2")
    return Fraction(1) - Fraction(cube_sum(profile) - n, n ** 3 - n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The two canonical profiles
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def dyadic_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """D_b = (2^(b-1), 2^(b-2), ..., 2, 1, 1), of mass 2^b."""
    return [2 ** (b - 1 - k) for k in range(b)] + [1]


def binomial_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """B_b = (C(b,0), ..., C(b,b)), of mass 2^b."""
    return [comb(b, j) for j in range(b + 1)]


def franel(b: int) -> int:
    """The b-th Franel number, sum_j C(b,j)^3 = cube sum of B_b."""
    return sum(comb(b, j) ** 3 for j in range(b + 1))


def dyadic_ceiling_closed_form(b: int) -> Fraction:
    """(6/7) * (1 + 1 / (2^b (2^b + 1)))."""
    n = 2 ** b
    return Fraction(6, 7) * (Fraction(1) + Fraction(1, n * (n + 1)))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Window profiles, computed two ways
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def window_profile_bruteforce(start: int, s: int) -> List[int]:
    """Trailing-zero tie profile of [start, start + 2^s) by enumeration.

    Blocks are indexed by k = 0..s-1 (exactly k trailing zeros) plus one
    'cap' block collecting the unique multiple of 2^s in the window.
    Cost Theta(2^s) -- use only for small s.
    """
    blocks = [0] * (s + 1)
    for x in range(start, start + 2 ** s):
        if x == 0 or x % (2 ** s) == 0:
            blocks[s] += 1
            continue
        k = trailing_zeros(x)
        if k >= s:
            blocks[s] += 1
        else:
            blocks[k] += 1
    return blocks


def window_profile_closed_form(s: int) -> List[int]:
    """Trailing-zero tie profile of any window of 2^s consecutive integers.

    Independent of the starting point (translation invariance): cost O(s).
    """
    return dyadic_profile(s)


def exact_bitlen_zero_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """Trailing-zero profile of the integers of exact bit-length b+1."""
    return window_profile_bruteforce(2 ** b, b)


def exact_bitlen_popcount_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """Popcount profile of the integers of exact bit-length b+1."""
    return profile_of([popcount(x) for x in range(2 ** b, 2 ** (b + 1))])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Inversion criterion
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def inversion_holds(b: int) -> bool:
    """True iff the popcount ceiling strictly exceeds the trailing-zero one.

    Equivalent arithmetic criterion: 7 * franel(b) < 8^b + 6.
    """
    return 7 * franel(b) < 8 ** b + 6


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. A Monte-Carlo check that the ceiling is a real ceiling
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def spearman(xs: Sequence[float], ys: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Spearman rank correlation with mid-ranks for ties."""

    def midranks(vs: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
        order = sorted(range(len(vs)), key=lambda i: vs[i])
        ranks = [0.0] * len(vs)
        i = 0
        while i < len(order):
            j = i
            while j + 1 < len(order) and vs[order[j + 1]] == vs[order[i]]:
                j += 1
            avg = (i + j) / 2.0 + 1.0
            for t in range(i, j + 1):
                ranks[order[t]] = avg
            i = j + 1
        return ranks

    rx, ry = midranks(xs), midranks(ys)
    n = len(xs)
    mx, my = sum(rx) / n, sum(ry) / n
    num = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(rx, ry))
    dx = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in rx) ** 0.5
    dy = sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in ry) ** 0.5
    return num / (dx * dy) if dx > 0 and dy > 0 else 0.0


def monte_carlo_ceiling(s: int, trials: int, seed: int) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Empirical max |rho| over random responses, and rho for the best response.

    Returns (best_random_rho2, order_compatible_rho2) on the window [0, 2^s).
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    xs = list(range(1, 2 ** s))  # drop 0 to keep nu_2 finite
    tvals = [trailing_zeros(x) for x in xs]
    best_random = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        ys = [rng.random() for _ in xs]
        best_random = max(best_random, spearman(tvals, ys) ** 2)
    # order-compatible response: strictly increasing in T, arbitrary inside ties
    ideal = [t + rng.random() for t in tvals]
    return best_random, spearman(tvals, ideal) ** 2

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from fractions import Fraction
from math import comb
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Basic statistics
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def trailing_zeros(x: int) -> int:
    """The 2-adic valuation nu_2(x): number of trailing binary zeros.

    By convention nu_2(0) is treated as 'maximal' by the caller; here we
    return the number of trailing zeros of the binary expansion, and 0 is
    handled explicitly by the profile routines.
    """
    if x == 0:
        raise ValueError("nu_2(0) is infinite; handle 0 separately")
    return (x & -x).bit_length() - 1


def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    """Number of one-bits in the binary expansion of x."""
    return bin(x).count("1")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Tie profiles and the Spearman ceiling
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def profile_of(values: Sequence[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Tie profile: the sorted list of fibre sizes of a statistic's values."""
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for v in values:
        counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1
    return [counts[k] for k in sorted(counts)]


def cube_sum(profile: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Sum of cubes of the block sizes."""
    return sum(m ** 3 for m in profile)


def spearman_ceiling(profile: Sequence[int]) -> Fraction:
    """Maximal attainable squared Spearman coefficient for this tie profile.

    Sp(L) = 1 - (sum_j m_j^3 - n) / (n^3 - n),  n = sum_j m_j >= 2.
    """
    n = sum(profile)
    if n < 2:
        raise ValueError("profile mass must be at least 2")
    return Fraction(1) - Fraction(cube_sum(profile) - n, n ** 3 - n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The two canonical profiles
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def dyadic_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """D_b = (2^(b-1), 2^(b-2), ..., 2, 1, 1), of mass 2^b."""
    return [2 ** (b - 1 - k) for k in range(b)] + [1]


def binomial_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """B_b = (C(b,0), ..., C(b,b)), of mass 2^b."""
    return [comb(b, j) for j in range(b + 1)]


def franel(b: int) -> int:
    """The b-th Franel number, sum_j C(b,j)^3 = cube sum of B_b."""
    return sum(comb(b, j) ** 3 for j in range(b + 1))


def dyadic_ceiling_closed_form(b: int) -> Fraction:
    """(6/7) * (1 + 1 / (2^b (2^b + 1)))."""
    n = 2 ** b
    return Fraction(6, 7) * (Fraction(1) + Fraction(1, n * (n + 1)))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Window profiles, computed two ways
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def window_profile_bruteforce(start: int, s: int) -> List[int]:
    """Trailing-zero tie profile of [start, start + 2^s) by enumeration.

    Blocks are indexed by k = 0..s-1 (exactly k trailing zeros) plus one
    'cap' block collecting the unique multiple of 2^s in the window.
    Cost Theta(2^s) -- use only for small s.
    """
    blocks = [0] * (s + 1)
    for x in range(start, start + 2 ** s):
        if x == 0 or x % (2 ** s) == 0:
            blocks[s] += 1
            continue
        k = trailing_zeros(x)
        if k >= s:
            blocks[s] += 1
        else:
            blocks[k] += 1
    return blocks


def window_profile_closed_form(s: int) -> List[int]:
    """Trailing-zero tie profile of any window of 2^s consecutive integers.

    Independent of the starting point (translation invariance): cost O(s).
    """
    return dyadic_profile(s)


def exact_bitlen_zero_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """Trailing-zero profile of the integers of exact bit-length b+1."""
    return window_profile_bruteforce(2 ** b, b)


def exact_bitlen_popcount_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """Popcount profile of the integers of exact bit-length b+1."""
    return profile_of([popcount(x) for x in range(2 ** b, 2 ** (b + 1))])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Inversion criterion
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def inversion_holds(b: int) -> bool:
    """True iff the popcount ceiling strictly exceeds the trailing-zero one.

    Equivalent arithmetic criterion: 7 * franel(b) < 8^b + 6.
    """
    return 7 * franel(b) < 8 ** b + 6


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. A Monte-Carlo check that the ceiling is a real ceiling
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def spearman(xs: Sequence[float], ys: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Spearman rank correlation with mid-ranks for ties."""

    def midranks(vs: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
        order = sorted(range(len(vs)), key=lambda i: vs[i])
        ranks = [0.0] * len(vs)
        i = 0
        while i < len(order):
            j = i
            while j + 1 < len(order) and vs[order[j + 1]] == vs[order[i]]:
                j += 1
            avg = (i + j) / 2.0 + 1.0
            for t in range(i, j + 1):
                ranks[order[t]] = avg
            i = j + 1
        return ranks

    rx, ry = midranks(xs), midranks(ys)
    n = len(xs)
    mx, my = sum(rx) / n, sum(ry) / n
    num = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(rx, ry))
    dx = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in rx) ** 0.5
    dy = sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in ry) ** 0.5
    return num / (dx * dy) if dx > 0 and dy > 0 else 0.0


def monte_carlo_ceiling(s: int, trials: int, seed: int) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Empirical max |rho| over random responses, and rho for the best response.

    Returns (best_random_rho2, order_compatible_rho2) on the window [0, 2^s).
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    xs = list(range(1, 2 ** s))  # drop 0 to keep nu_2 finite
    tvals = [trailing_zeros(x) for x in xs]
    best_random = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        ys = [rng.random() for _ in xs]
        best_random = max(best_random, spearman(tvals, ys) ** 2)
    # order-compatible response: strictly increasing in T, arbitrary inside ties
    ideal = [t + rng.random() for t in tvals]
    return best_random, spearman(tvals, ideal) ** 2

  }

  "interactive_layout": "# A Guided Tour: The Dial That Refuses to Move

*How a one-instruction statistic — "how many binary zeros does this number end with?" — turns out to have a rank-correlation ceiling that is completely immune to where you sample, how big your numbers are, and how you condition your draws.*

---

## 1. The question

Suppose a computational pipeline turns each integer input $x$ into a number, a *rate*, and you want to know how much of that rate is predicted by something cheap about $x$. Two candidates cost one machine instruction each:

- the **trailing-zero statistic** $T(x) = \nu_2(x)$: the largest $k$ with $2^k \mid x$. For $x = 12 = 1100_2$, $T = 2$.
- the **popcount baseline** $W(x)$: the number of one-bits. For $x = 12$, $W = 2$.

A measurement on integers drawn uniformly among those of exactly 48 bits — that is, uniformly on $[2^{47}, 2^{48})$ — reports Spearman rank correlations of
$$0.7291, \qquad 0.7286, \qquad 0.7087$$
across three independent seeds, with the trailing-zero statistic beating the popcount baseline by $+0.134$.

Before believing any of that, a sceptic asks: **how much of this is just the arithmetic of the statistic?** $T$ is enormously coarse — half of all integers have $T = 0$, a quarter have $T = 1$, and so on. Massive ties cap rank correlation. Maybe $0.73$ is simply the ceiling.

Answering that question turns out to require a small theory, and the theory is prettier than the measurement.

---

## 2. Ties, ranks, and the price of coarseness

<details><summary><b>Background: what Spearman correlation does with ties</b> (click to expand)</summary>

Spearman's $\rho$ is Pearson correlation applied to ranks. When a statistic takes the same value on several sample points, those points must share a rank — conventionally the average of the ranks they would have occupied. Sharing ranks shrinks the variance of the rank vector, and a shrunken variance caps the correlation.

Concretely: if the statistic partitions a sample of $n$ points into tied blocks of sizes $m_1, \ldots, m_r$, the rank vector has variance $\frac{n^3-n}{12} - \frac{1}{12}\sum_j(m_j^3 - m_j)$ rather than the untied $\frac{n^3-n}{12}$. Cauchy–Schwarz against any response's rank vector then gives the bound below, with equality when the response is untied and orders the sample compatibly with the statistic.

See also the general background on [rank correlation coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spearman%27s_rank_correlation_coefficient).
</details>

**Definition (tie profile).** The *tie profile* of a statistic on a sample of size $n$ is the list of fibre sizes $(m_1,\ldots,m_r)$, $\sum_j m_j = n$. Its *mass* is $n$ and its *cube sum* is $C = \sum_j m_j^3$.

**Theorem (ceiling).** No matter what response you correlate against, the squared Spearman coefficient obeys
$$\rho^2 \;\le\; \mathrm{Sp} \;=\; 1 - \frac{C - n}{n^3 - n},$$
and this is attained by any response strictly increasing in the statistic.

Two profiles of the same mass are therefore compared purely by cube sums — **and the comparison reverses**: bigger cube sum, smaller ceiling. Hold on to that; it is the lever that makes everything else work.

---

## 3. Play with it: the sliding window laboratory

Here is the central empirical claim, made interactive. Choose a scale $s$ and a starting point $A$; the widget enumerates the window $\{A, \ldots, A + 2^s - 1\}$, counts how many of its members end in exactly $k$ binary zeros for each $k$, and compares with the prediction. Try aligned starts, wildly unaligned starts, huge starts, $A = 2^s$ (the exact-bit-length window). Try to break it.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

You cannot break it. The profile is always
$$D_s = (2^{s-1},\, 2^{s-2},\, \ldots,\, 2,\, 1,\, 1),$$
and the ceiling always $\frac{6}{7}\big(1 + \frac{1}{2^s(2^s+1)}\big)$.

---

## 4. Why $6/7$?

Once you know the profile is $D_b$, the ceiling is a geometric series away.

The cube sum is $\sum_{k<b} 8^{\,b-1-k} + 1 = \frac{8^b-1}{7} + 1$, and the mass is $n = 2^b$.

<details><summary><b>Click to reveal the two-line computation</b></summary>

With $n = 2^b$ and $C = \frac{n^3-1}{7}+1$:
$$C - n = \frac{n^3 - 7n + 6}{7} = \frac{(n-1)(n-2)(n+3)}{7}, \qquad n^3 - n = n(n-1)(n+1),$$
so
$$\mathrm{Sp}(D_b) = 1 - \frac{(n-2)(n+3)}{7n(n+1)} = \frac{6(n^2+n+1)}{7n(n+1)} = \frac{6}{7}\left(1 + \frac{1}{n(n+1)}\right).$$
</details>

**Theorem (closed-form ceiling).** For $b \ge 1$,
$$\mathrm{Sp}(D_b) = \frac{6}{7}\left(1 + \frac{1}{2^b(2^b+1)}\right), \qquad\text{so}\qquad \rho_{\max} \to \sqrt{6/7} = 0.9258201\ldots$$
with the correction below $4^{-b}$ — smaller than $10^{-28}$ at $b = 47$.

The picture below shows the profile's geometric halving and the ferocious speed of that convergence.

{{visualization:0}}

**Immediate consequence.** The measured $0.73$ is nowhere near $0.9258$; the value is not saturation. And the measured *decline* with bit-length, roughly $0.78 \to 0.72 \to 0.65 \to 0.61$, cannot be the ceiling drifting: the ceiling moves by less than $10^{-28}$ across that whole range.

---

## 5. Why placement cannot matter

The widget's stubbornness has a one-line explanation, and it is not the one most people reach for first.

**The tempting argument (alignment).** For a window $[c\cdot 2^s, (c+1)\cdot 2^s)$ aligned to the dyadic grid, adding $c\cdot2^s$ to a number changes nothing about divisibility by $2^k$ or $2^{k+1}$ when $k < s$, because $2^{k+1}$ divides $2^s$. So translation is an explicit bijection between the blocks of $[0,2^s)$ and those of the window.

That is correct, transparent — and proves too little. It leaves you expecting that *unaligned* windows are perturbed at order $2^{-s}$.

**The right argument (period divisibility).**

<details><summary><b>Click to reveal the general proof</b></summary>

Two facts:

1. Having exactly $k$ trailing zeros is a *single residue class*: $\nu_2(x) = k \iff x \equiv 2^k \pmod{2^{k+1}}$. (If $x = 2^{k+1}q + 2^k = 2^k(2q+1)$ then $2^k \mid x$, $2^{k+1}\nmid x$; conversely $x = 2^k(2q+1) = 2^{k+1}q + 2^k$.)
2. A run of $M\cdot r$ consecutive integers meets each residue class mod $r$ exactly $M$ times, because it is a disjoint union of $M$ complete residue systems.

Now write $2^s = 2^{s-1-k}\cdot 2^{k+1}$ and apply (2) with $r = 2^{k+1}$, $M = 2^{s-1-k}$: every window of $2^s$ consecutive integers contains exactly $2^{s-1-k}$ numbers with $\nu_2 = k$, for each $k < s$. Apply (2) again with $r = 2^s$, $M = 1$: exactly one multiple of $2^s$. Total $2^{s-1} + \cdots + 2 + 1 + 1 = 2^s$, so the window is exhausted and the profile is exactly $D_s$. There is no error term.
</details>

**Theorem (translation invariance).** For every start $A$ and every scale $s$, the window $\{A, \ldots, A+2^s-1\}$ has trailing-zero tie profile exactly $D_s$.

So the ceiling is a function of the **sample size** alone: not of the integers' magnitude, not of alignment, not of placement, not of bit-length conditioning. Here is the same statement as a deliberately boring picture — a heat map of deviations that is identically zero:

{{visualization:2}}

And here is the $O(s)$ algorithm that this theorem licenses: it computes the profile of a scale-47 window without touching any of its $2^{47}$ elements.

---

## 6. Conditioning on the bit-length costs exactly one bit

The measurement did not sample from $[0,2^{48})$; it sampled from $[2^{47}, 2^{48})$, forcing the top bit on. That is a different measure, so it needs its own bookkeeping.

**Theorem (one-bit shift law).** The trailing-zero tie profile of uniform draws at exact bit-length $b+1$ is exactly $D_b$: the full-range profile *one bit lower*. And the popcount profile of the same draws is exactly $B_b = \big(\binom{b}{0},\ldots,\binom{b}{b}\big)$, the full-range binomial profile one bit lower.

<details><summary><b>Click to reveal both proofs</b></summary>

*Trailing zeros.* The $k$-th block of $[2^b,2^{b+1})$ is the set difference of the $k$-th blocks of $[0,2^{b+1})$ and $[0,2^b)$, of size $2^{b-k} - 2^{b-1-k} = 2^{b-1-k}$ for $k<b$. And an element divisible by $2^b$ in that window is $2^bu$ with $1 \le u < 2$, forcing $u = 1$: the single point $2^b$.

*Popcount.* Identify integers of exact bit-length $b+1$ with subsets $S$ of $\{0,\ldots,b\}$ containing the top index $b$. Then $S \mapsto S\setminus\{b\}$ is a bijection onto $j$-subsets of $\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$, so exactly $\binom{b}{j}$ of them have popcount $j+1$.
</details>

Both dials shift by exactly one bit, *simultaneously*. Every comparison between them therefore transports unchanged from bit-length $b$ to exact bit-length $b+1$. That is why the exact-bit-length-48 experiment can be analysed as a bit-length-47 one.

---

## 7. The showdown: which statistic has more headroom?

Both profiles have mass $2^b$. By the reversal principle of Section 2, the whole question is a cube-sum comparison:
$$C(D_b) = \frac{8^b - 1}{7} + 1 \qquad\text{versus}\qquad C(B_b) = \sum_{j=0}^{b}\binom{b}{j}^3 = \mathrm{franel}(b),$$
the [Franel numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franel_number) $1, 2, 10, 56, 346, 2252, \ldots$ Rearranged, the popcount baseline has the strictly higher ceiling exactly when
$$7\,\mathrm{franel}(b) < 8^b + 6.$$

Watch the race:

{{visualization:1}}

At $b = 1$: $14 = 14$. At $b = 2$: $70 = 70$ — and indeed $D_2 = (2,1,1)$ and $B_2 = (1,2,1)$ are permutations of each other, so they are tie-equivalent. At $b = 3$: $392 < 518$, and it never turns back.

**Theorem (exact inversion threshold).** For $b \ge 1$, the popcount baseline has strictly greater tie headroom than the trailing-zero statistic **if and only if $b \ge 3$**.

<details><summary><b>Click to reveal how the large-$b$ half is proved</b></summary>

Franel numbers have no elementary closed form, so one estimates. Bounding each $\binom{b}{j}^3$ by (row maximum)$^2\times\binom{b}{j}$ gives $\mathrm{franel}(b) \le \binom{b}{\lfloor b/2\rfloor}^2 2^b$. For odd $b = 2m+1$, Pascal's rule gives $\binom{2m+1}{m} = \binom{2m}{m-1} + \binom{2m}{m} \le 2\binom{2m}{m}$, and a central-binomial estimate $\binom{2m}{m}^2(3m+1) \le 16^m$ then yields
$$\mathrm{franel}(2m+1)\,(3m+1) \le 4\cdot 16^m\cdot 2^{2m+1} = 8^{2m+1}.$$
Any bound of the form $\mathrm{franel}(b)\cdot c \le 8^b$ converts into a ceiling bound $\mathrm{Sp}(B_b) \ge 1 - 2/c$, so for $m \ge 5$ the popcount ceiling is at least $1 - \frac{2}{3m+1} \ge \frac78$, which beats the trailing-zero envelope $\frac67 + 2^{-b}$. Below $b = 10$ the estimate is too lossy (at $b=8$ it gives only $0.846 < 6/7$), but there the cube sums are finite arithmetic and can just be checked.
</details>

The decision procedure, with both the exact and the asymptotic route:

And the exact-rational ceiling evaluator that turns a profile into a number:

**The punchline.** At exact bit-length 48 the tie geometry *favours the popcount baseline* — it has strictly more headroom. Yet the measurement puts the trailing-zero statistic $+0.134$ ahead. The measured advantage runs **against** the geometry. It cannot be a tie artefact.

## 9. What we learned

Line up the deflationary hypotheses:

| Hypothesis | Verdict |
|---|---|

  rw [h, pow_succ]

    rw [pow_succ] at hv

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from fractions import Fraction
from math import comb
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Basic statistics

def trailing_zeros(x: int) -> int:
    """The 2-adic valuation nu_2(x): number of trailing binary zeros.

    By convention nu_2(0) is treated as 'maximal' by the caller; here we
    return the number of trailing zeros of the binary expansion, and 0 is
    handled explicitly by the profile routines.
    """
    if x == 0:
        raise ValueError("nu_2(0) is infinite; handle 0 separately")
    return (x & -x).bit_length() - 1


def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    """Number of one-bits in the binary expansion of x."""
    return bin(x).count("1")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Tie profiles and the Spearman ceiling
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def profile_of(values: Sequence[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Tie profile: the sorted list of fibre sizes of a statistic's values."""
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for v in values:
        counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1
    return [counts[k] for k in sorted(counts)]


def cube_sum(profile: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Sum of cubes of the block sizes."""
    return sum(m ** 3 for m in profile)


def spearman_ceiling(profile: Sequence[int]) -> Fraction:
    """Maximal attainable squared Spearman coefficient for this tie profile.

    Sp(L) = 1 - (sum_j m_j^3 - n) / (n^3 - n),  n = sum_j m_j >= 2.
    """
    n = sum(profile)
    if n < 2:
        raise ValueError("profile mass must be at least 2")
    return Fraction(1) - Fraction(cube_sum(profile) - n, n ** 3 - n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The two canonical profiles
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def dyadic_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """D_b = (2^(b-1), 2^(b-2), ..., 2, 1, 1), of mass 2^b."""
    return [2 ** (b - 1 - k) for k in range(b)] + [1]


def binomial_profile(b: int) -> List[int]:
    """B_b = (C(b,0), ..., C(b,b)), of mass 2^b."""
    return [comb(b, j) for j in range(b + 1)]


def franel(b: int) -> int:
    """The b-th Franel number, sum_j C(b,j)^3 = cube sum of B_b."""
    return sum(comb(b, j) ** 3 for j in range(b + 1))


def dyadic_ceiling_closed_form(b: int) -> Fraction:
    """(6/7) * (1 + 1 / (2^b (2^b + 1)))."""
    n = 2 ** b
    return Fraction(6, 7) * (Fraction(1) + Fraction(1, n * (n + 1)))

def window_profile_bruteforce(start: int, s: int) -> List[int]:
    """Trailing-zero tie profile of [start, start + 2^s) by enumeration.

    Blocks are indexed by k = 0..s-1 (exactly k trailing zeros) plus one
    'cap' block collecting the unique multiple of 2^s in the window.
    Cost Theta(2^s) -- use only for small s.
    """
    blocks = [0] * (s + 1)
    for x in range(start, start + 2 ** s):

            blocks[s] += 1
            continue
        k = trailing_zeros(x)
        if k >= s:
            blocks[s] += 1
        else:
            blocks[k] += 1
    return blocks

    Independent of the starting point (translation invariance): cost O(s).

    """True iff the popcount ceiling strictly exceeds the trailing-zero one.

    Equivalent arithmetic criterion: 7 * franel(b) < 8^b + 6.

def spearman(xs: Sequence[float], ys: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Spearman rank correlation with mid-ranks for ties."""

    def midranks(vs: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
        order = sorted(range(len(vs)), key=lambda i: vs[i])
        ranks = [0.0] * len(vs)
        i = 0
        while i < len(order):
            j = i
            while j + 1 < len(order) and vs[order[j + 1]] == vs[order[i]]:
                j += 1
            avg = (i + j) / 2.0 + 1.0
            for t in range(i, j + 1):
                ranks[order[t]] = avg
            i = j + 1
        return ranks

    rx, ry = midranks(xs), midranks(ys)
    n = len(xs)
    mx, my = sum(rx) / n, sum(ry) / n
    num = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(rx, ry))
    dx = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in rx) ** 0.5
    dy = sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in ry) ** 0.5
    return num / (dx * dy) if dx > 0 and dy > 0 else 0.0


def monte_carlo_ceiling(s: int, trials: int, seed: int) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Empirical max |rho| over random responses, and rho for the best response.

    Returns (best_random_rho2, order_compatible_rho2) on the window [0, 2^s).
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    xs = list(range(1, 2 ** s))  # drop 0 to keep nu_2 finite
    tvals = [trailing_zeros(x) for x in xs]
    best_random = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        ys = [rng.random() for _ in xs]
        best_random = max(best_random, spearman(tvals, ys) ** 2)
    # order-compatible response: strictly increasing in T, arbitrary inside ties
    ideal = [t + rng.random() for t in tvals]
    return best_random, spearman(tvals, ideal) ** 2

import Novelty.ProbeRetentionLimits

/-!
# Why the hybrid arm cannot hurt, and when it helps (NET-69, interaction layer)

`Novelty.ProbeRetentionLimits` analysed a *single* score.  NET-69's third arm
mixes two: the accumulated heavy-hitter statistic `h` and the content probe `p`
are combined into `hybrid h p λ = h + λ · p`, and the measurement is that on
code the mixture is **non-degrading** (`0.9371` versus `0.9340` for `λ = 1`),
whereas on prose the same mixture harms monotonically.  This file explains that
asymmetry structurally.

* `isTopSet_hybrid_iff` — the selection `S` survives the mixture iff a *linear*
  system in `λ` holds, one inequality per retained/discarded pair.
* `hybrid_isTopSet_of_margin` — hence an explicit **non-degradation threshold**:
  if the accumulated score separates `S` from its complement by a margin `γ` and
  the probe has oscillation at most `D`, then every `λ ≤ γ/D` leaves the
  selection, and therefore the retained mass, untouched.  Non-degradation is a
  margin phenomenon, not a property of the probe's accuracy.
* `hybrid_stability_convex` and `hybrid_stability_ordConnected` — the set of
  mixing weights that preserve a given selection is an **interval** containing
  every weight between any two of its members.  This is the structural reason a
  domain can only exhibit *monotone* harm: once `λ` leaves the stability
  interval of the accumulated selection it never re-enters it.
(The uniqueness lemma `eq_of_isTopSet_of_strict` of `Novelty.ProbeRetentionLimits`
makes the numerical instances below unambiguous.)

Section 3 contains two fully explicit four-key instances, both verified
numerically before being formalised (see `ComputationalEvidence.md`).

* `accuracy_does_not_order_retention` — a score that is **four times more
  accurate** in `L²` (`SSE = 150` versus `1802`) retains **nineteen times less**
  mass (`1` versus `19`).  Prediction accuracy does not order retention even
  weakly; this is the counterexample that blocks the naive reading "the probe
  arm loses because its `R²` is low", and it is the exact companion of
  `exists_probe_perfect_retention_with_Rsq`.
* `hybrid_strictly_beats_both_arms` — an instance in the NET-69 régime where the
  accumulated arm retains `11`, the probe-only arm `9`, and the `λ = 1` hybrid
  `19`: strictly more than either parent.  So the measured `+0.3` points are not
  noise-shaped luck; a mixture can strictly dominate both arms because the two
  scores misrank *different* pairs.
* `hybrid_stability_threshold_example` — for that instance the stability
  interval of the accumulated selection is exactly `[0, 2/5]`, and the mixture
  helps precisely because `λ = 1` lies outside it.  Deployment corollary:
  choosing `λ` below the margin ratio guarantees safety but also guarantees the
  hybrid learns nothing from the probe.

Section 4 closes the loop on the *pessimism* of the transfer theorems:

* `sup_transfer_bound_is_sharp` — a four-key instance attaining the constant
  `2Bε` of `retained_ge_of_isTopSet_sup` exactly.  The bound cannot be improved,
  so the gulf between it and the `R²`-perfect probe of
  `exists_probe_perfect_retention_with_Rsq` is real: `L∞`/`L²` accuracy pins
  down retention only up to the full worst case.
-/

namespace Catalog.Novelty.ProbeHybridStability

open Finset Catalog.Novelty.ProbeRetentionLimits

variable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]

/-! ### 1. The mixture and its stability interval -/

/-- The hybrid score: accumulated statistic `h` mixed with content probe `p` at
weight `lam`. -/
def hybrid (h p : ι → ℝ) (lam : ℝ) : ι → ℝ := fun i => h i + lam * p i

omit [Fintype ι] in
@[simp] lemma hybrid_zero (h p : ι → ℝ) : hybrid h p 0 = h := by
  funext i; simp [hybrid]

omit [Fintype ι] in
/-- The mixture keeps a selection iff a linear system in the mixing weight
holds: one inequality per (retained, discarded) pair. -/

/-!
# The knee is a lower bound for *every* eviction policy (NET-67 ⋈ NET-69)

`Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee` (round 21, NET-67) studies the knee
`knee p τ = sInf {k | τ ≤ ∑_{i<k} p i}` of a *sorted* attention profile: the
number of keys the top-`k` policy needs in order to reach the drift-assert
threshold `τ`.  `Novelty.ProbeRetentionLimits` (round 22, NET-69) studies
arbitrary budget-`B` selection rules driven by a score.  This file joins them.

The bridge is the observation that, for a sorted profile, the **prefix is a top
set** in the sense of NET-69 (`isTopSet_prefixSel`).  Everything follows:

* `retained_le_retained_prefix` — no budget-`B` policy, however clever, retains
  more mass than the prefix of length `B`.  The NET-67 retention curve is thus
  not merely the curve of one heuristic; it is the *envelope* of all policies.
* `retained_lt_of_card_lt_knee` — below the knee **every** policy misses the
  threshold.  The knee is therefore a hard budget floor, not an artefact of
  top-`k` eviction: reporting `12/16` keys for code (NET-68) is reporting a
  quantity no scoring rule can beat.
* `knee_le_of_reaches` — the contrapositive, in the form used experimentally:
  an arm that passes the drift assert at budget `B` certifies `knee ≤ B`.
* `probe_at_knee_budget` — the NET-69 arms re-enter: a score with `L∞` error `ε`
  run at any budget `B ≥ knee p τ` still retains at least `τ - 2Bε`.  Combined
  with the sharpness instance `sup_transfer_bound_is_sharp`, this is the exact
  price of content-blindness: a weak probe costs mass at most linearly in the
  budget and its error, and that linear rate is attained.
-/

namespace Catalog.Novelty.ProbeKneeBridge

open Finset Catalog.Novelty.ProbeRetentionLimits

variable {n k B : ℕ} {p : ℕ → ℝ} {tau : ℝ}

/-- The importance vector that a sorted profile `p` induces on a context of `n`
keys. -/
def keyMass (p : ℕ → ℝ) (n : ℕ) : Fin n → ℝ := fun i => p (i : ℕ)

/-- The prefix selection: the `k` best-ranked keys of an `n`-key context. -/
def prefixSel (n k : ℕ) (h : k ≤ n) : Finset (Fin n) :=
  (Finset.range k).attachFin fun _ hm => lt_of_lt_of_le (Finset.mem_range.mp hm) h

@[simp] lemma card_prefixSel (h : k ≤ n) : (prefixSel n k h).card = k := by
  simp [prefixSel, Finset.card_attachFin]

lemma mem_prefixSel {h : k ≤ n} {i : Fin n} : i ∈ prefixSel n k h ↔ (i : ℕ) < k := by
  simp [prefixSel, Finset.mem_attachFin]

/-- The two notions of retained mass agree on prefixes: the NET-67 retention
curve is the NET-69 retained mass of the prefix selection. -/
lemma retained_prefixSel (h : k ≤ n) :
    retained (keyMass p n) (prefixSel n k h)
      = Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.retained p k := by
  refine Finset.sum_bij' (fun (i : Fin n) _ => (i : ℕ))
    (fun m hm => (⟨m, lt_of_lt_of_le (Finset.mem_range.mp hm) h⟩ : Fin n)) ?_ ?_ ?_ ?_ ?_
  · intro a ha; exact (Finset.mem_attachFin _).mp ha
  · intro m hm; exact (Finset.mem_attachFin _).mpr (by simpa using hm)
  · intro a _; rfl
  · intro m _; rfl
  · intro a _; rfl

/-- **The prefix of a sorted profile is a top set.**  This is the bridge: the
NET-67 top-`k` policy is exactly the oracle policy of NET-69. -/
theorem isTopSet_prefixSel (hp : Antitone p) (h : k ≤ n) :
    IsTopSet (keyMass p n) k (prefixSel n k h) := by
  refine ⟨card_prefixSel h, fun i hi j hj => ?_⟩
  have hik : (i : ℕ) < k := mem_prefixSel.mp hi
  have hjk : ¬ ((j : ℕ) < k) := fun hc => hj (mem_prefixSel.mpr hc)
  exact hp (le_of_lt (lt_of_lt_of_le hik (not_lt.mp hjk)))

/-- **The retention curve is the envelope of all policies.**  No budget-`k`
selection retains more mass than the prefix of length `k`. -/
theorem retained_le_retained_prefix (hp : Antitone p) (h : k ≤ n) {S : Finset (Fin n)}
    (hS : S.card = k) :
    retained (keyMass p n) S ≤ Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.retained p k := by
  rw [← retained_prefixSel (p := p) h]
  exact retained_le_of_isTopSet_true (isTopSet_prefixSel hp h) hS

/-- **Below the knee every policy fails.**  If the budget is smaller than the
knee then no scoring rule whatsoever reaches the drift-assert threshold: the
knee is a hard floor on the key budget, not a property of top-`k` eviction. -/
theorem retained_lt_of_card_lt_knee (hp : Antitone p) (hB : B ≤ n)
    (hlt : B < Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.knee p tau) {S : Finset (Fin n)}
    (hS : S.card = B) : retained (keyMass p n) S < tau :=
  lt_of_le_of_lt (retained_le_retained_prefix hp hB hS)
    (Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.lt_knee hlt)

/-- The experimentally used contrapositive: an arm that passes the drift assert
at budget `B` certifies that the knee is at most `B`. -/
theorem knee_le_of_reaches (hp : Antitone p) (hB : B ≤ n) {S : Finset (Fin n)}
    (hS : S.card = B) (hreach : tau ≤ retained (keyMass p n) S) :
    Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.knee p tau ≤ B := by
  by_contra hc
  exact absurd hreach (not_le.mpr (retained_lt_of_card_lt_knee hp hB (not_le.mp hc) hS))

/-- **The price of content-blindness.**  A score with `L∞` error `ε`, run at any
budget at least the knee, still reaches the threshold up to `2Bε`.  With
`sup_transfer_bound_is_sharp` (which attains `2Bε`) this pins the cost of a weak
probe exactly: linear in the budget and in the error, and no better.  Note that
sortedness of the profile is *not* needed here — only the threshold reachability
supplied by the knee. -/
theorem probe_at_knee_budget {s : Fin n → ℝ} {ε : ℝ}
    (hnn : ∀ i, 0 ≤ p i) (hB : B ≤ n)
    (hknee : Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.knee p tau ≤ B)
    (hex : ∃ m, tau ≤ Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.retained p m)
    {S : Finset (Fin n)} (hS : IsTopSet s B S) (hε : ∀ i, |keyMass p n i - s i| ≤ ε) :
    tau - 2 * B * ε ≤ retained (keyMass p n) S := by
  have hthr : tau ≤ Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.retained p B :=
    le_trans (Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.knee_spec hex)
      (Catalog.Novelty.AttentionRetentionKnee.retained_mono hnn hknee)
  have htrans := retained_ge_of_isTopSet_sup (a := keyMass p n) (s := s)
    hS (card_prefixSel (n := n) (k := B) hB) hε
  rw [retained_prefixSel (p := p) hB] at htrans
  linarith

end Catalog.Novelty.ProbeKneeBridge
